title: Minimum Increment Operations to Make Array Beautiful
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` of length `n` and an integer `k`. A single operation adds 1 to the value at any one index you like, and you may apply as many operations as you want, including none.

The array counts as **beautiful** when every contiguous stretch of three or more elements holds at least one value that is `k` or larger. Return the smallest number of operations after which `nums` is beautiful.
notes:
## Intuition

A stretch of four or more elements always contains a stretch of exactly three, so the rule only has to hold for every window of three neighbours. Partly raising a value never helps: a value either ends at least `k` (and then raising it exactly to `k` is cheapest, costing `max(0, k - nums[i])`) or it is left alone. So the task is to choose "tall" positions so that no three neighbours are all short, with the smallest total cost. Trying every set of positions is exponential; a left-to-right DP is linear.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i]` be the cheapest way to fix the prefix ending at `i` when position `i` itself is tall.
2. For each `i`, `cost` is what it takes to lift `nums[i]` to `k` (zero if it is already there).
3. The previous tall position must be one of `i - 1`, `i - 2` or `i - 3`; otherwise three short values sit in a row. For `i < 3` no earlier tall position is needed, so `previous` is 0.
4. `dp[i] = cost + previous`.
5. The last tall position must be among the final three indices, so return the smallest of `dp[n - 1]`, `dp[n - 2]`, `dp[n - 3]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 3, 0, 0, 2]`, `k = 4`, so the costs are `[2, 1, 4, 4, 2]`.

- `dp[0] = 2`, `dp[1] = 1`, `dp[2] = 4` (no predecessor needed).
- `dp[3] = 4 + min(4, 1, 2) = 5`.
- `dp[4] = 2 + min(5, 4, 1) = 3`.

The answer is `min(dp[4], dp[3], dp[2]) = min(3, 5, 4) = 3`: lift index 1 and index 4.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), one constant-time step per index.
- Space: O(n) for `dp`; keeping only the last three values would make it O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Checking only windows of exactly three is enough; checking longer ones adds nothing.
- The answer can reach about 3.3 · 10^13, so in Java or C it needs a 64-bit type.
- Do not return `dp[n - 1]` alone: the last element does not have to be tall.
- With `k = 0` every cost is zero and the answer is 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `dp[i]` | least operations for the prefix up to `i` with `nums[i]` raised to at least `k` |
| `cost` | operations needed to lift `nums[i]` to `k` |
| `previous` | cheapest `dp` among the three positions before `i` (0 when `i < 3`) |

narration.2: Remember the length of the array.
narration.3: dp[i] will hold the cheapest fix of the prefix ending at i when nums[i] is made at least k.
narration.5: Visit every index from left to right.
narration.6: Lifting nums[i] to exactly k costs k - nums[i], or nothing if it is already high enough.
narration.7: Among the first three indices no earlier tall value is required, so the carried cost starts at 0.
narration.8: From index 3 on, the previous tall value must be at most three steps back.
narration.9: Take the cheapest of the three possible previous tall positions.
narration.11: The cost for a tall i is its own lift plus the best way to cover everything before it.
narration.14: The last tall value must sit in the final three positions, so the answer is the smallest of those three dp values.
